assistant.content:
Below is a sample set of “discreet” but compliant camera-placement points, followed by key legal and best-practice reminders.  Adjust as needed for your floor plan and local regulations.

1. Exterior Entrances  
   • Above the front porch or overhang, angled down at the main door.  
   • At the back door or sliding-glass door, mounted under the eaves.  
   Purpose: deter break-ins, verify comings/goings, no audio needed.

2. Driveway / Parking Area  
   • On a pole, fence post or exterior wall, covering drive or carport.  
   Purpose: vehicle safety, guest arrival/departure timestamps.

3. Outdoor Amenity Spaces  
   • Patio, pool deck or grill area—mounted high under eaves or on a corner post.  
   Purpose: liability protection, crowd control; keep cameras 8–10 ft up so guests don’t feel watched at eye-level.

4. Main Indoor Entry Corridor  
   • High on a wall or in a corner of the hallway leading from front door → living area.  
   Purpose: track entry/exit, package deliveries; camera body should be plainly visible to satisfy “reasonable expectation of privacy.”

5. Common-Area Living Room  
   • Discreetly in a ceiling corner or on a high shelf.  
   Purpose: monitor emergencies (fire, break-in); no audio recording or full-room pan/tilt is generally safest.

6. Stairwell or Landing (if multi-level)  
   • Mounted above the first/last step, facing downward.  
   Purpose: fall/injury documentation, unauthorized access control.

General Placement Tips  
 • Mount cameras at 8–10 feet high; angle down slightly.  
 • Choose lenses with 90°–120° field of view to avoid excessive room coverage.  
 • Use privacy-masking features (“privacy zones”) to block off adjoining private areas (e.g. neighbor’s yard).  
 • Favor fixed cameras over pan/tilt to limit over-surveillance.  

What to Avoid  
 • Any camera inside bedrooms, bathrooms or closets.  
 • Hidden/covert cameras—these violate most jurisdictions’ laws and Airbnb policy.  
 • Audio recording except where expressly allowed by local wiretap statutes and with guest consent.

Legal & Policy Considerations  
 1. Jurisdictional Privacy Laws  
    – U.S.: federal Wiretap Act, plus state “two-party consent” rules (CA, FL, PA, MA, etc.).  
    – EU/UK: GDPR requires a legal basis (legitimate interest), data-protection impact assessment, limited retention.  
    – Other regions: check local surveillance, data-privacy, and landlord-tenant statutes.  

 2. Airbnb Rules  
    – All security cameras must be disclosed in your listing under “Safety & property” → “Security cameras.”  
    – Cameras may not be placed inside private spaces.  
    – Guests must have “reasonable expectation of privacy” in all non-public areas.  

 3. Signage & Disclosure  
    – Post a small sign (e.g. near the front door) noting “24/7 video surveillance in common areas.”  
    – Include a line in your house rules and online listing. Transparency builds trust.

 4. Data Handling Best Practices  
    – Encryption at rest + in transit; strong authentication on camera accounts.  
    – Retention limits (30 days is common) unless needed for an incident.  
    – Clear policy for who can view footage and under what circumstances.  

By limiting cameras to exterior doors, driveways, and public/common areas—and by fully disclosing their presence—you strike a balance between guest safety, property protection, and legal compliance.
